detail.abstract:
What happens to the value of teaching professional English writing to non-native speakers when AI can translate their native-language work into polished English? This paper addresses this question through a case study of AI-assisted translation and develops a broader framework for understanding the relocation of human expertise in AI-mediated intellectual work. 

We model writing as a communication protocol in which the author must ensure that the reader can reconstruct the intended meaning accurately and efficiently. Hypothesizing a Chinese professor who develops a scientific manuscript in Chinese and relies on AI for an English version, we identify a structural gap in the traditional writing workflow: AI can assume the production of polished English, but the author may no longer possess the language expertise required to independently verify the resulting communication. The traditional self-editing loop breaks. 

We argue that the central problem is not the disappearance of human expertise, but its relocation from first-draft production to first-line verification. Drawing on historical divisions of intellectual labor, Bryan Garner's editorial framework, and examples from mathematics and other domains, we generalize this insight into a verification-ladder model in which AI assumes production and lower-level verification, while human expertise moves toward higher-level verification and authorization. 

The paper concludes that AI-era education should focus not on competing with machine drafts, but on preserving the human capacity to inspect, challenge, revise, and take responsibility for AI-mediated communication. More broadly, as AI assumes more of the intellectual workflow, human expertise will increasingly re-anchor itself at higher tiers of verification and non-delegable authorization.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) innovation advances faster than organizations can adapt, and customer service is one setting in which such friction becomes visible. detail.abstract: We describe a deployed system that simulates the reasoning of consumer segments by conditioning large language models on curated, segment-specific evidence drawn from population-scale consumer data. This is a systems and design paper: we report the architecture, the rationale for each component, and a preliminary internal audit of concept traceability. Comparative validation against human research benchmarks is specified but not reported here. The architecture makes four commitments. First, segments are represented multi-dimensionally, and each penetration-based variable, whatever its source, carries two values: index (distinctiveness relative to the reference population) and penetration (prevalence within the segment), giving one reasoning grammar across otherwise incompatible source formats. Second, generation is concept-first: the concepts the stimulus raises are established before retrieval and before the answer is written, and they constrain both, so that a variable is admitted to the rationale only where it maps to a concept the question raised. Third, a two-lane retrieval layer assembles a question-specific variable batch for each turn rather than passing the full catalog, moving responsibility for model attention into a separately testable component. Fourth, each response carries a structured record, completed once the answer is written, of the concepts addressed, the variables drawn on for each, and a self-reported source mix, retained with the session so that the derivation can be inspected afterward. We claim auditability rather than accuracy: the record makes a derivation checkable against the underlying data, which is a different property from agreement with human respondents. The target is an aggregate, directional signal at the segment level, not a simulation of any individual. We state the question types the method is offered for-attitudinal and motivational questions, concept reactions, trade-off simulations-and those it is not: behavioral measurement, precise share-of-choice estimation, and longitudinal tracking.

detail.abstract:
Leadership teams have been assessed for decades through psychometric instruments, behavioural surveys, interviews, 360-degree feedback, team diagnostics and normative benchmarks. The field has become increasingly sophisticated, and several established methodologies explicitly address collective phenomena such as alignment, trust, decision-making, accountability, adaptability and team effectiveness. Yet a prior question remains insufficiently separated from questions of reliability, scale and benchmarking: what exactly is the signal being measured?
This paper argues that different leadership-team assessments can produce apparently comparable collective scores while relying on fundamentally different evidence architectures. Some ask team members to rate the team directly. Some aggregate individual personality or behavioural profiles. Some triangulate psychometrics, interviews, 360-degree or stakeholder input, behavioural observation and expert judgment. Others construct collective properties from structured individual inputs through explicit transformation rules. These approaches may all be useful, but they do not observe the same object, and the richness or scale of the evidence does not remove the need to identify what inference the resulting signal can legitimately support. 
A central distinction follows. A subjective perception is data, and convergence among multiple perceptions can be empirically meaningful. Aggregation may reduce idiosyncratic noise, reveal agreement and support reliable comparison. Benchmarking may show how a team differs from a reference population. But aggregation and scale do not, by themselves, change the epistemic nature of the original signal. More observations can make a subjective measure more statistically stable; they cannot, by their number alone, make it objective.
The paper further argues that the assessment industry's long history creates a second question. Decades of use and thousands of assessed teams demonstrate adoption, operational feasibility and, in some cases, reliability or association with selected outcomes. They do not automatically establish that a measure corresponds to the collective execution phenomenon invoked in high-stakes settings such as due diligence, transformation and value creation. The relevant evidential question is therefore not only where the signal came from, but where it went: was it confronted with independently observable operating reality? 
PHCI® is presented as one alternative architecture. It does not claim objective ground truth. It uses structured individual inputs to construct explicit group-level signals, connects them to execution related and strategic-readiness interpretations, and proposes in-situ operational concordance as an evidential discipline: freeze the signal, confront it with observable facts, retain counterevidence, and re-measure the same collective over time. The broader argument is not that perception-based methods are invalid. It is that measurement quality begins with clarity about what is observed, how the collective signal is constructed, and what evidence is allowed to challenge the inference.

detail.abstract: This paper is written to investigate the shift in ideologies in the wealth management industry of the Asia Pacific region, especially focusing on the financial hubs of Hong Kong and Singapore. detail.abstract: Work-from-home (WFH) arrangements have become an increasingly relevant approach to workplace management as organizations seek to maintain service delivery, employee productivity, and operational continuity while providing greater flexibility in how work is performed. In this context, the present study examined the relationship between the Friday WFH arrangement and employee productivity among employees of a government agency in the Philippines. The study employed a quantitative descriptivecorrelational research design and included 83 qualified employees, of whom 73 provided valid responses for the final analysis after excluding 10 questionnaires during data screening. Data were gathered through a validated structured questionnaire administered primarily through Google Forms, with printed questionnaires provided when necessary, and analyzed using frequency, percentage, weighted mean, and Pearson product-moment correlation. The findings revealed that the Friday WFH arrangement was generally implemented favorably, while employee productivity was assessed at a very high level across all dimensions. All five dimensions of the Friday WFH arrangement showed positive and statistically significant relationships with employee productivity, leading to the rejection of the null hypothesis. Flexibility in performing work tasks demonstrated the strongest relationship with productivity. Respondents generally disagreed that they experienced the identified challenges, although work-related and technical challenges and work environment and personal challenges received relatively higher assessments than the other challenge dimensions. Based on these findings, the study proposed a WFH productivity enhancement program to strengthen work resources and equipment, communication and coordination, monitoring and supervision, flexibility in performing work tasks, technical support, and employees' home working conditions. The findings support the Job Demands-Resources Theory by highlighting the relevance of job resources, including flexibility, communication, supervision, scheduling, and adequate work resources, to employee productivity in a remote-work setting. Practically, the study provides a basis for sustaining supportive WFH practices, addressing identified areas for improvement, and promoting consistent employee productivity, accountability, and operational continuity.

detail.abstract: Temporary fare suspension may help maintain mobility during disasters, but little is known about how riders respond to such policies. This study examines who increased transit use during the fare-free period following the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires, whether riders made trips only because fares were suspended, and which travel modes they replaced with transit. detail.abstract: This paper applies the frameworks of total surplus analysis and inclusive wealth indexing to quantify the net economic wealth lost to psychosocial stress triggered by environmental change, using proximity to a proposed or operational nuclear waste deposit as the exemplar. Conventional GDP measures may record some market transactions associated with stress-related healthcare expenditure or property-value adjustment, yet they substantially understate the triangular losses in consumer and producer surplus that arise from reduced longevity, stigma-driven demand shifts, and foregone ecosystem-service benefits. Formalised as a negative shift in total surplus, where stress induces a leftward or downward movement in the marginal social benefit curve-through nocebo effects, anticipatory anxiety and perceived health risks-and an upward shift in marginal social costthrough accelerated biological ageing and behavioural sequelae-the analysis finds a large negative net surplus even at negligible radiological doses. Drawing on psychoneuroendocrinology, telomere biology, and hedonic and inclusive-wealth valuation, including ETH Zürich-affiliated ecosystem restoration and natural-capital accounting, the empirical ranges assembled here (0.5-3 years of reduced life expectancy; quality-adjusted life years monetised at CHF 100,000-200,000; property-value depressions of 10-30 per cent; and tourism and recreational benefits foregone) imply cumulative wealth destruction in the tens to hundreds of billions of Swiss francs, in present value, for a mid-sized Swiss or European siting scenario. Total surplus and inclusive wealth are argued to dominate GDP as metrics for perceived environmental risk. Transparent risk communication and community engagement, which dampen nocebo amplification, have a correspondingly high economic return.

detail.abstract: Public cancer research funding is routinely described as disconnected from disease burden. detail.abstract: A growing share of business commerce could be transacted through AI agents that verify rather than trust. This paper treats that machine counterparty as a limit case: because it extends no benefit of the doubt to a claim it cannot check, it strips out the human tolerances (relationship, reputation by impression, the reluctance to verify) on which much of marketing has quietly depended and so makes the structure of defensibility visible. Read through the Commoditization Stack, whatever a generative system can produce is neither rare nor inimitable, so commoditization runs in two orders, of digital-marketing output and of the marketing activity itself, and differentiation migrates to a non-synthesizable residue: institutional anchoring, meaning brand as accumulated trust, accreditation, certification, and nameable accountability, on the layers that resist rather than erode. The human case is then the same structure with tolerance added, not the normal case from which machines deviate. The account converts into instruments for the builder: a defensibility test that separates the erodible from the residue, a Minimum Viable Hypothesis discipline that requires falsification and human evidence before capital, and a reading of homologated networks where verification is already a lookup. Digital marketing emerges as the layer through which that residue is made legible, to a person and increasingly to a machine. Because no actor attests itself, defensibility is borrowed across nested scales, from the professional to the firm, the university, the region, and the country, so the university is the professional's balance sheet rather than a bystander. A further contribution follows: because the competence this requires cannot be exercised without understanding the systems it addresses, the paper treats AI literacy as a structural input at two levels, functional and critical formation for practice and mechanistic depth for research and reads marketing's differential in machine-to-machine negotiation as verifiable and attested signal rather than persuasion. detail.abstract: Electrification is often framed as replacing fossil fuels with low-carbon electricity, but that understates the change. Deep electrification is a regime shift: fossil systems are organised around extractable fuels, combustion and inventories, with fuel costs dominating, while a highly electrified renewable system is organised around infrastructure and energy flows, with electricity as the main carrier, more efficient end uses, supply variability, and balancing via storage, demand flexibility and interconnection. This reorganisation has two defining structural consequences. First, primary energy demand falls substantially as electrification eliminates the combustion and conversion losses embedded throughout fossil systems. The same useful services are delivered with far less total energy input. Second, the visible infrastructure footprint expands, at least temporarily, because electrification requires a larger electricity system, more dependent on capturing diffuse natural flows. Although in the longer term electrification replaces several parallel fossil energy systems (gas networks, liquid fuel supply chains and solid fuel logistics), during the mid-transition, old and new systems coexist, so the infrastructure burden peaks before fossil assets are retired. In the long run, net physical infrastructure most likely declines. Seeing electrification as a regime change clarifies these structural features and shows that the central challenge is not just cleaner molecules but reorganising the energy system from a commodity paradigm, organised around fuel stocks and markets, to an infrastructure and time-coordination paradigm.

Patent offices worldwide—including the Five IP Offices (USPTO, EPO, JPO, CNIPA, and IPO) and WIPO national phase receiving administrations—face a chronic backlog crisis driven by inflating pendency rates and rising examination costs. This paper identifies the primary, unaddressed structural driver of this crisis: 'moving-target searching.' Under prevailing administrative workflows, scientific patent examiners are routinely deployed to conduct labor-intensive, global prior art searches (e.g., US 35 U.S.C. §§ 102/103, EPC Articles 54/56) on patent applications that suffer from preliminary informalities, ambiguous claim scope, or non-elected multiple inventions. When applicants subsequently amend or restrict these un-clarified claims during prosecution, the examiner's initial search is rendered obsolete, forcing costly, iterative re-searches.

To eliminate this systemic inefficiency, this paper proposes an institutional administrative framework: The Two-Stage Examination Firewall. Under Stage 1, non-examiner administrative screening officers (clerks) execute strict formal verification, fee audits, formatting checks, and mandatory restriction/unity elections to formally lock claim boundaries prior to search assignment. Only when an application's claim scope is certified as clear, unified, and procedurally compliant does it pass through the firewall to Stage 2, where a scientific examiner executes a single, high-precision prior art search. Through comparative workflow analysis across the IP5 offices and WIPO PCT national phase procedures, supported by quantitative efficiency modeling, this study proves that decoupling clerical boundary locking from substantive prior art search eliminates 30–40% of wasted examiner search hours, compresses Office Action cycles from 3–4 down to 1–2, and slashes global examination pendency without requiring statutory amendments to national patent acts.

detail.abstract: The Sudanese civil war that erupted in 2023 pushed the national economy into a historic collapse, with inflation surging to 256% in 2023 and real GDP contracting by approximately 29.4% (World Bank, 2026; International Monetary Fund, 2026). Against this backdrop, the Port Sudan authorities explored joining the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) as a potential pathway to circumvent dollar shortages and reduce inflation. Drawing on the empirical experience of 15 countries that joined CIPS between 2015 and 2026, and applying the International Monetary Fund (IMF) exchange rate pass-through model (International Monetary Fund, 2012; Central Bank of Sudan, n.d.), this paper systematically assesses the feasibility of Sudan's accession to CIPS. The study finds that CIPS success requires the simultaneous satisfaction of four preconditions: relative political stability, an export basket to China, central bank enforcement will, and technological infrastructure modernization. However, the April 2026 explicit rejection by the U.S. Treasury of the Port Sudan authorities' application—conditioned on ending the war, achieving peace, and forming a civilian-led transitional government (Al Arabiya, 2026; Alsulta, 2026)—fundamentally alters the assessment framework. Under this constraint, the projected success rate of CIPS plummets from 65–70% to less than 10%, while the probability of failure rises from 60–75% to over 90%. The paper's core argument is that CIPS is a necessary but not sufficient condition; without political settlement, Sudan's core risk is not liberation from the dollar trap but the substitution of a dollar-denominated predicament with a yuan-denominated one (Eichengreen, 2011; Prasad, 2014; Cohen, 2015). The correct policy sequence should be: peace first, civilian government second, financial reintegration third, and CIPS diversification last.

detail.abstract: Human dignity is among the most frequently invoked and most frequently criticised concepts in contemporary constitutional and human rights law. Its textual presence in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, in the German Basic Law, in the Brazilian Constitution of 1988 and in the South African Constitution contrasts with persistent disagreement about its philosophical ground and its legal content. This article asks how legal orders connect philosophical accounts of dignity to enforceable human rights norms, and whether the concept meaningfully constrains adjudication. Using doctrinal, comparative and jurisprudential analysis of international instruments and of leading decisions from Germany, South Africa, Brazil, the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union, with the United States as a contrasting case, it examines the existing literature, identifies a gap between work on dignity's content and work on its institutional role, and develops a central thesis: that dignity performs three analytically separable functions in law (foundational, interpretive and adjudicative), that philosophical disagreement is disabling mainly in the third, and that legal convergence across jurisdictions is better explained by shared intermediate specifications than by agreement on foundations. The article addresses the strongest objections, namely that dignity is redundant, that it is culturally parochial, and that it licenses unstructured judicial discretion, and states conditions under which the thesis would fail. It concludes with a modest standard of judicial reasoning, the specification requirement, and discusses its institutional feasibility. The contribution is doctrinal, comparative and normative; it is not empirical, and its limits are stated.

detail.abstract: Fifth-generation (5G) networks are expected to serve enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency, and massive machine-type communications over a shared physical infrastructure, and network slicing is the architectural mechanism that makes this plurality possible. Comparative tables and figures synthesize study scope, learning methods, and unresolved challenges. The review identifies recurring gaps, including limited use of operator-grade data, weak treatment of safety and constraint satisfaction during online learning, thin evaluation of multi-domain slices, and scarce attention to explainability and lifecycle governance. In response, a conceptual hybrid framework is proposed that couples a forecasting layer, a constrained DRL decision layer, and an assurance layer within an SDN/NFV-compatible control loop. The framework is a research proposal and has not been experimentally validated here. The paper closes with practical implications for operators and a research agenda covering offline learning, federated coordination, and standardized benchmarks.

detail.abstract: We adapt Two-Sided Projected Principal Component Analysis (TIP-PCA), a forecasting method originally developed for intraday volatility, to yield curve forecasting. The dynamic Nelson-Siegel (DNS) model, a standard benchmark, fixes the shape of its term-structure factors in advance and predicts each factor only from its own past. TIP-PCA removes both restrictions, estimating the maturity-side structure and the month-to-month dynamics nonparametrically, the latter driven by covariates built from past yield levels. This lets us build covariates from short, mid, and long maturity segments instead of the whole curve. Segmentation substantially improves accuracy over whole-curve covariates. With the rank set to three as in DNS, TIP-PCA attains lower RMSE than DNS, AR(1), and a random walk at the oneand three-month horizons. The gain over DNS is significant mainly at one month. At longer horizons, TIP-PCA does not improve on DNS, except marginally at twelve months with a validated rank. At rank three, the gains come mainly from the month-to-month dynamics rather than from estimating the maturity-side loadings, and run through more accurate slopefactor forecasts. The gains over DNS also widen in turmoil such as the 2007-2009 financial crisis and the recent high-inflation period, when DNS forecasts lag the yield curve while the flexible models track it more closely.

detail.abstract: American higher education is confronting an era of unprecedented legal, regulatory, financial, and political change. This symposium introduction situates the challenges of the 2020s within the historical evolution of higher education law and highlights the significant developments reshaping colleges and universities. These include the consequences of Loper Bright for federal administrative authority, fundamental changes to collegiate athletics and student-athlete compensation, revisions to federal financial aid programs, increasing institutional closures and consolidations, evolving First Amendment concerns, and the growing role of lawyers in university leadership. The essay introduces the symposium contributions addressing these issues while examining their broader implications for institutional governance, compliance, financial sustainability, and educational mission. Together, the articles demonstrate that higher education leaders must navigate an increasingly complex intersection of law, politics, economics, and public expectations. Despite these pressures, the essay argues that the current disruption also presents an opportunity for institutional renewal. Forward-looking leadership, informed by legal and regulatory expertise and grounded in higher education’s enduring commitments to learning, social mobility, and civic life, will be essential to navigating change while preserving and reimagining the sector’s fundamental purposes.

detail.abstract: Shafer's evidence theory is a branch of the mathematics of uncertain reasoning that allows for novel possibilities to be conceived by a decision-maker. Many of its findings exhibit striking similarities with an alternative decision theory purported by Shackle in the 1950s, before expected utility maximisation monopolised the scene. Evidence theory does not attempt to formalise the emergence of novelties, but it is a suitable framework for reconstructing the formation of beliefs when novelties appear. An application to decisionmaking in the biotech and pharmaceutical industry illustrates the potentialities of evidence theory, as well as its shortcomings.

detail.abstract: The modernization of digital payment systems is becoming increasingly important to financial integration and economic activity across the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Instant payment systems can improve the speed with which funds are transferred, while interoperability allows users connected to different financial institutions and payment networks to transact with one another. Together, these capabilities can reduce fragmentation and strengthen the infrastructure supporting cross-border financial activity. This conceptual article examines the role of interoperability in instant payment systems and its contribution to digital payment modernization across ECOWAS. It explores how instant and interoperable payment infrastructure can influence transaction speed, accessibility, cost, reliability, financial inclusion, and regional financial integration. The article also examines regulatory coordination, settlement infrastructure, technical standards, cybersecurity, data governance, and institutional cooperation as conditions affecting successful implementation. It argues that instant payment infrastructure can provide significant benefits when supported by interoperable networks and compatible institutional arrangements, but speed alone does not guarantee efficient cross-border payments. Sustainable modernization requires coordination between technology, regulation, financial institutions, and payment users. The article concludes that interoperable instant payment systems can strengthen regional financial integration when developed as part of a coordinated digital financial infrastructure strategy across ECOWAS.

detail.abstract:
Achieving long-term operational efficiency at the Indian Patent Office (IPO) requires restoring the statutory distinction between preliminary formalities and substantive examination. Grounded in general patent jurisprudence and the statutory scheme of Section 12(1) of the Patents Act, 1970, patent evaluation operates across three distinct tiers: Level 1 (Definitional Completeness under Section 2(1)(j)), Level 2 (Statutory Subject-Matter Filters under Sections 3 and 4), and Level 3 (Substantive Prior-Art Patentability under Section 13 and Section 2(1)(ja)). Under prevailing prosecution practice, Examiners routinely execute Level 3 prior art searches [Section 12(1)(c)] while Level 1 and Level 2 formal defects, ambiguous claim scope, or multi-invention disclosures [Section 12(1)(a)/(b)] remain unresolved. Commingling preliminary clerical defects with substantive prior art rejections in First Examination Reports (FERs) forces scientific Examiners to act as proofreaders while conducting premature, "moving-target" searches that must be re-run when claims are subsequently restricted or clarified.

Serving as the India-specific companion study to The Two-Stage Examination Firewall: A Global Policy Blueprint for Eliminating Moving-Target Searches and Slashing Patent Pendency across IP5 Offices (Arora, 2026, SSRN Abstract ID: 7552458), this paper deconstructs the legislative history of the 1959 Ayyangar Committee Report (Paras 388 & 404) to demonstrate that Parliament intended preliminary compliance to be achieved before activating substantive prior art searching. To operationalize this statutory design without legislative amendment, this study proposes a Two-Stage Administrative Architecture: Stage 1 establishes a Preliminary Formalities & Boundary Gate where non-examiner administrative clerks clear pure formal defects under Section 12(1)(a) (without priority penalties), while statutory tools such as Section 17(2) re-dating are deployed strictly when pre-search amendments alter disclosure scope. Stage 2 reserves scientific Examiners exclusively for single-pass Level 3 prior art searches under Section 13 on boundary-locked claim sets—eliminating redundant search iterations, compressing pendency, and boosting IPO disposal throughput by 30–40%.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effects of floods on firms, combining their financial information and exact location with administrative data on floods at the municipality level between 2004 and 2024 in France. For firms located in municipalities hit by a flood, both survival rates and sales deteriorate: their chances of survival drop by 2%, and their sales by 8%, for up to five years after the event. Moreover, these firms are more likely to relocate to safer areas in other municipalities. These effects are driven by intense floods, lasting at least one week. We find evidence of both direct and indirect effects: firms in 1-in-100 years floodplain are more affected than others, but even floods occurring in neighboring municipalities decrease firms’ economic performance, with magnitudes attenuating as distance increases.

detail.abstract: We study attitudes towards climate policies in Russia. For international comparability, we build on the survey experiment of Dechezleprêtre et al. (2025), adapting it to the Russian context and adding treatments that reference the national Climate Doctrine. Russians' climate beliefs and knowledge broadly mirror those in other countries, although skepticism is higher in fossil-fuel-rich regions. Physics-based video increases factual understanding, while policy-based messaging reduces willingness to undertake personal emission-reducing actions, consistent with a cost-salience channel. Formal messages from political authorities do not change people's views on whether climate change is real, but they do increase people's willingness to fight climate change.

title: Circularity and Sustainability under Biophysical Constraints: a Macro–Materials Framework
affiliations: Imperial College London and University of Pisa

detail.title: Circularity and Sustainability under Biophysical Constraints: a Macro–Materials Framework
detail.abstract: This paper develops a simple analytical macro–materials model to examine the feasibility of circular economies under biophysical constraints. Economic output depends on refined-metal throughput supplied through primary extraction, recycling, and recovery from discard stocks. We derive explicit conditions linking circularity, material sustainability, and extraction dependence, showing that high recycling intensity is neither necessary nor sufficient for sustainability because stronger recovery loops may destabilize stock dynamics if not moderated by depreciation and demographic dilution forces. Extending the framework to account for energy requirements further shows that materially sustainable equilibria may nevertheless become energetically infeasible over time as extraction energy intensity rises. A calibration to global copper and zinc cycles reproduces observed differences in circularity performance across materials and illustrates how increases in energy intensities due to declining ore grades may generate finite energetic sustainability horizons under constrained low-carbon energy availability.

detail.abstract: Multi-modal medical image fusion synthesizes complementary anatomical and functional information into a single image. Yet two practical bottlenecks remain. First, different modality pairs (e.g., CT-MRI vs. PET-MRI) reflect distinct imaging physics, so a single static parameterization can induce gradient conflict, whereas fully task-specific models incur parameter redundancy. Second, task-specific specialization is often data-limited, making full fine-tuning vulnerable to overfitting and degradation of transferable representations.We propose PA-MoEFusion, a two-stage Generalist--Specialist framework to address both dilemmas. In the generalist pre-training stage, a Physics-Aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module constructs imaging-physics-inspired gating descriptors from spatial gradient and frequency-domain energy distributions. It dynamically routes heterogeneous modality features to multiple decoupled differential convolution experts---Central Difference (CD) for edge preservation, Angular Difference (AD) for orientation, Radial Difference (RD) for symmetric patterns, and standard Convolution (CV) as a baseline---achieving efficient cross-task feature disentanglement and interpretable routing. A learned prior generator and stop-gradient decoupling further stabilize the routing against co-adaptation collapse. In the specialist fine-tuning stage, the generalist backbone is frozen and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules are inserted, updating only 4.8\% of the model parameters to specialize the pretrained generalist under limited paired training data.Evaluated on the Harvard Medical Dataset (CT-MRI, PET-MRI, SPECT-MRI), PA-MoEFusion (0.83M parameters) obtains the best or second-best score on 17 of 18 metric--task combinations among the compared methods. Under 50%-data few-shot conditions in our protocol, LoRA adaptation outperforms full fine-tuning across the reported metrics, supporting parameter-efficient adaptation under limited paired data.

detail.abstract: Using a monthly security-level dataset, this paper reconstructs market size, composition, and equity returns for Alexandria, Cairo, and Istanbul. By 1913, equity capitalization reached 40% of GDP in Egypt but 14% in Ottoman Turkey. Growth came through new issuance rather than price appreciation, while risk-adjusted returns were low. Istanbul co-moved more strongly with London, reflecting foreign-incorporated mining and banking firms linked to international capital markets, while Egypt’s larger market was concentrated in land and mortgage finance tied to its cotton economy. The findings show that legal regimes governing foreign capital shaped how peripheral exchanges interacted with global financial markets.

title: Depth-Adaptive Channel Competitive Inhibition and Calibration-Aware Training for Interpretable Medical Image Classification
affiliations: Independent Researcher, Independent Researcher and Federal Medical Center Ebute-metta

detail.title: Depth-Adaptive Channel Competitive Inhibition and Calibration-Aware Training for Interpretable Medical Image Classification
detail.abstract: Lateral inhibition in biological visual cortex decreases in strength from early to late processing areas, implementing a depth-adaptive gain-control gradient that sharpens feature selection at input stages while preserving distributed representations at higher levels. Convolutional neural networks use channel attention mechanisms that apply uniform reweighting at every depth, failing to model this biologically-motivated property as a learned architectural feature. Standard cross-entropy training also produces overconfident softmax outputs that undermine uncertainty-based decision routing, a well-documented failure mode of deep classifiers. We introduce two contributions to address these gaps. First, Depth-Adaptive Inhibition Scheduling (DAIS), which extends Learnable Channel Competitive Inhibition (LCCI) with a learnable per-depth scaling parameter δd. Training without ordering constraint consistently produces δ₁ = 0.707 ± 0.023 > δ₂ = 0.675 ± 0.015 across all three training seeds on malaria microscopy images, and δ₁ = 0.697 ± 0.004 > δ₂ = 0.686 ± 0.004 on chest X-ray images. This cross-modal consistency, confirmed in 3/3 seeds on both imaging modalities, is a novel learned hierarchical property of CNN feature selection that mirrors the depth-dependent lateral inhibition gradient observed in biological visual cortex. Second, Calibration-Aware Training (CAL), a joint objective L = LCE + λ·ECE that trains calibration as an architectural property, reducing inter-seed F1 variance by 42%. We validate on the NIH Malaria Cell Images Dataset (27,558 cells, N = 4,134 test set) using three-seed evaluation with McNemar exact test and TOST, achieving F1 = 96.52% ± 0.32% (95% CI [96.16, 96.88]) and AUROC = 99.31% ± 0.08%. A six-variant ablation confirms all components are performance-neutral, consistent with their purpose as interpretability contributions. CBAM-ResNet-50 significantly outperforms our method (p = 0.008, ΔF1 = -1.05%); we report this without selective framing. ​
